fields.expected: I submitted my jobright-application-agent, a local browser agent I built in TypeScript and Node that handles the repetitive parts of job applications: discovering roles, opening ATS pages, filling repeated fields, and tracking state. I deliberately built it as a deterministic, operator-controlled agent rather than a general autonomous one, because a single wrong action can submit a real application or fabricate an answer. Every application moves through an explicit state machine (DISCOVERED through SUBMITTED and OUTREACH), with SQLite as the single source of truth so state cannot diverge across processes, and Zod validating anything crossing a boundary. Mutating capabilities sit behind fail-closed flags like SUBMIT_ENABLED that never default on. I also built a validation ladder, from UNIT_CONFIRMED up to LIVE_MUTATION_CONFIRMED, so a capability is not called working just because it passes against a fixture. Free-text essays and demographic fields are architecturally blocked from autofill and always generate a human-review item. It supports Greenhouse fully, Lever and Ashby partially, and intentionally skips Workday and iCIMS rather than handling them unreliably. Dispatch, a React operator console, runs and approves the pipeline. It reflects how I think about agents: the boundary between machine action and human judgment should be explicit.

fields.expected: I care about the gap between an agent that can take an action and an agent that should. Replit's platform lets people build real applications from natural language, which means the agent is writing, running, and shipping code on someone's behalf. That is exactly the design problem I spent months on with my job-application agent: every mutating capability sat behind fail-closed flags like SUBMIT_ENABLED, state moved through an explicit machine rather than ad hoc edits, and I built a validation ladder from UNIT_CONFIRMED up to LIVE_MUTATION_CONFIRMED so a capability could not be called working just because it passed against a local fixture. I also built an operator console so a human could observe and approve the pipeline instead of trusting it blindly. Separately, my Intelehealth work evaluating LLM outputs against a 4,169-case clinical benchmark convinced me that generating output is cheap and deciding whether to trust it is the hard part. Replit is one of the few places where agent reliability, developer tooling, and a large real user base are the same problem, and I want to own pieces of that system rather than isolated tickets.
